title: Start Here: Why Candles?
subtitle: Fire, focus and the element of Fire in magic
intro: Candles are probably the most common tool in modern witchcraft, and for good reason. They are cheap, easy to find, and they hold a living flame that changes as you watch it. Lighting a candle is a clear, physical signal to your mind that ordinary time has stopped and magical time has begun.

In Western elemental systems, the flame belongs to Fire, the element of will, courage, passion, transformation and change. Fire takes one thing (wax and wick) and turns it into light, heat and smoke. Many practitioners see a candle spell the same way: your intention goes into the candle, and as it burns, that intention is released and set in motion. A candle also holds all four elements at once, since the solid wax is Earth, the melted wax is Water, the air feeds the flame and the flame itself is Fire.

Candle magic shows up in many traditions, from Wicca and eclectic witchcraft to European folk practice, Catholic devotional candles, and hoodoo rootwork, the African American folk magic tradition that has shaped much of the candle work sold in spiritual supply shops today. You do not need to follow any one of these to begin. This section starts with the basics: choosing, preparing, timing, burning and reading candles, and doing all of it safely.
keyIdeas: A candle gives your intention a visible focus, and watching the flame helps hold your attention on one goal.
The flame is associated with the element of Fire: will, energy, courage, passion and transformation.
Many practitioners see a burning candle as releasing the intention placed in it, a little more with every minute it burns.
Color, carving, oil, herbs and timing are layers you can add, but a plain white candle and a clear intention are enough to start.
Candle magic appears across many traditions, including hoodoo, which is a living African American tradition worth learning about with respect.
Action in the everyday world is part of the spell. The candle supports your effort; it does not replace it.
Fire is real fire. Safety habits are part of good practice, not an afterthought.

practice.name: A First Candle Meditation
steps: Choose a plain white tealight or chime candle and set it in a sturdy holder on a heatproof plate, at least 12 inches from anything that can burn.
Sit comfortably, tie back long hair and loose sleeves, and take three slow breaths to settle.
Hold the unlit candle for a moment and think of one simple, positive intention, such as "I welcome calm into my evening."
Set the candle down, light it, and say your intention aloud or silently.
Rest your gaze softly on the flame for three to five minutes. Notice its color, height and movement without trying to change anything.
When your mind wanders, gently bring it back to the flame and your intention.
Thank the flame, the element of Fire, or simply yourself, in whatever words feel right.
Snuff the candle with a snuffer or a lid rather than leaving it to burn while you do something else.
Write the date, your intention and anything you noticed about the flame in your journal.

variations.name: Electric candle version
variations.text: If you live in a dorm, rental or home where open flames are not allowed, an LED candle still works as a focus. Many practitioners pair it with an image of a flame or a written intention placed under it.

variations.name: Elements on the altar
variations.text: Place a stone (Earth), a feather or incense (Air), a small bowl of water (Water) and your candle (Fire) together, and spend a moment greeting each one before you light the flame.

variations.name: Nightly gratitude flame
variations.text: Light a tealight each evening for ten minutes while you list three things you are grateful for, then snuff it. Over a few weeks the ritual itself becomes a powerful cue for calm.

tools: A plain white tealight or chime candle
A sturdy candle holder and a heatproof plate or tray
Matches or a lighter
A candle snuffer or metal lid
Your journal or this app's journals

correspondences.label: Element
correspondences.value: Fire: will, courage, passion, energy, transformation

correspondences.label: Direction
correspondences.value: South in many Western traditions (this varies by tradition and hemisphere)

correspondences.label: Colors
correspondences.value: Red, orange and gold for Fire; white as an all-purpose candle

correspondences.label: Crystals
correspondences.value: Carnelian and sunstone for fiery energy, clear quartz for focus

correspondences.label: Herbs and resins
correspondences.value: Cinnamon and dragon's blood, associated with Fire and power

correspondences.label: Symbols
correspondences.value: The upward-pointing triangle, the alchemical symbol for Fire

signs: You find it easier to settle and focus once the candle is lit.
Lighting a candle starts to feel like a signal that practice time has begun.
You begin to notice small differences in how flames behave from night to night.
pitfalls: Thinking you need special or expensive candles to start. A plain white candle works for nearly anything.
Lighting a candle and then walking away. The flame should stay in your sight the whole time it burns.
Expecting the candle to do all the work. Pair your spell with real-world steps toward your goal.
Reading too much into every flicker. Drafts and wick length explain a lot, as you will learn in the lesson on reading the flame.
safety: Never leave a burning candle unattended or burning while you sleep. Use a sturdy holder on a heatproof plate or tray, keep it at least 12 inches from curtains, paper, plants and anything that can burn, and keep it out of reach of children and pets. Tie back long hair and loose sleeves before you light a flame, ventilate the room, and keep a snuffer or lid nearby. Candle work can support your wellbeing, but it is not a substitute for medical, legal or mental health care.

title: Choosing a Candle
subtitle: Types, waxes, sizes and burn times
intro: The candle you choose shapes the spell. A tiny tealight suits a quick blessing, while a tall glass-jar candle suits a working that unfolds over a week. Size matters because burn time matters: many practitioners want a spell candle to burn completely, across one sitting or several, so picking the right size keeps the spell practical and safe.

The most common spell candles are tealights, chime or spell candles, tapers, pillars, glass-jar 7-day candles, and figure candles shaped like people, animals or symbols. Each has its own strengths. Chime candles are small and burn in an evening, tapers are elegant and easy to carve, pillars are sturdy for long workings, and jar candles are popular in hoodoo and devotional practice for steady, multi-day work.

Wax matters too. Beeswax is natural, burns long and bright, and is often considered the most traditional and "alive" choice. Paraffin is inexpensive and comes in every color, but can be sootier. Soy is plant-based and burns cool, but is soft, so it works best in containers. There is no wrong choice, only what fits your budget, values and spell.
keyIdeas: Tealights burn about 3 to 5 hours and suit quick blessings, meditations and small daily work.
Chime or spell candles (about 4 inches tall and 1/2 inch wide) burn about 1 1/2 to 2 hours, so a whole spell fits in one sitting.
Tapers (8 to 12 inches) burn roughly an hour per inch, about 6 to 12 hours in total, and are easy to carve and dress.
Pillars burn for many hours (a 3 by 6 inch pillar often lasts 50 to 80 hours) and suit workings repeated over days or weeks.
Glass-jar 7-day candles hold roughly 100 to 120 hours of burn time and are a staple of hoodoo and devotional candle work.
Figure candles (human, cat, skull, seven-knob and others) add a symbolic shape and usually burn a few hours to an evening.
Beeswax is long-burning and natural, paraffin is cheap and colorful, and soy is plant-based but soft and best in a container.

practice.name: Matching a Candle to a Spell
steps: Write down one intention you want to work on, such as better focus at work.
Decide how many sessions you want: one evening, three nights, seven days, or a full moon cycle.
Estimate how long you can safely watch each session, for example one hour a night.
Multiply sessions by time to find the burn time you need, then choose a candle type that matches it from the key ideas above.
Choose a color that fits your intention, or white if you are unsure.
Pick a wax that fits your values and budget, and check that you have a holder that fits the candle snugly.
Look the candle over for cracks, a bent or buried wick, or a tilt that could make it burn unevenly.
Note your choice and your reasons in your journal, so you can compare how different candles worked for you over time.

variations.name: Seven-knob candle
variations.text: A candle shaped as seven stacked knobs is traditionally burned one knob per day for seven days, with a wish or petition repeated each time. Snuff it after each knob.

variations.name: Birthday candle wishes
variations.text: Tiny birthday candles burn in minutes, which makes them handy for very small workings or when you only have a few minutes to watch a flame.

variations.name: Devotional jar candle
variations.text: Many people burn a glass-jar candle in honor of a saint, deity or ancestor, lighting it for a while each day. Some carefully decorate the outside of the glass with paint markers before lighting.

tools: A selection of candles: tealights, chime candles, tapers, a pillar or jar candle
Holders that fit each candle securely
A heatproof plate or tray
A ruler, to estimate taper burn time
Your journal

signs: Your candles burn out close to when you expected, so spells finish on schedule.
You stop buying candles you never use and start reaching for the same reliable types.
You notice which waxes give you the cleanest, steadiest flame.
pitfalls: Choosing a large pillar for a one-night spell and then feeling you must leave it burning. Pick a size you can watch.

Using a holder that is too loose or too small, so the candle leans or falls.
Burning tealights without their metal cup or setting them directly on wood or plastic.
safety: Burn times are only estimates, so never leave any candle burning unattended or while you sleep, even a long-burning jar or pillar. Glass-jar 7-day candles can crack or shatter when hot, so set them on a heatproof surface, never in a window, and do not let them burn dry; stop when about 1/2 inch of wax remains. Keep tealights in their metal cups on a heatproof plate, use holders that fit snugly, keep every candle at least 12 inches from anything that can burn, and keep candles out of reach of children and pets.

title: Candle Colors and Their Meanings
subtitle: A full color guide, and why white works for anything
intro: Color is one of the easiest ways to tune a candle to your intention. Most practitioners match the candle's color to the goal: green for money and growth, pink for affection, black for protection and banishing, and so on. These meanings come from a mix of sources, including European folk magic, Western astrology and ceremonial magic, and hoodoo rootwork, and they do not always agree.

That disagreement is normal. In some traditions purple is about psychic power, while in hoodoo it is often tied to mastery and command. Some witches use blue for healing and others prefer green. The table in this lesson gives widely used meanings, but your own associations count too. If red feels like protection to you because of your family or culture, that link has real power in your work.

White is the universal candle. Many practitioners treat white as containing all colors, the way white light holds the whole spectrum, so a white candle can stand in for any other color. If you cannot find a gold candle for a success spell, a white one with clear intention, a carved symbol or a dab of a matching oil works perfectly well.
keyIdeas: Match the candle color to your intention to add one more layer of focus to the spell.
Color meanings vary between traditions, and your personal and cultural associations are valid.
White can substitute for any color, because many practitioners see it as holding all colors at once.
Black is not "evil"; most practitioners use it for protection, banishing and absorbing negativity.
Colors can also be chosen by planet, day of the week, element or sabbat.
Dyed wax can sometimes burn sootier than plain wax, so color-through or overdipped candles may behave differently.

practice.name: Building Your Personal Color Key
steps: Open a new journal page titled "My Candle Colors."
List the fourteen colors from the correspondence table in this lesson, leaving space beside each one.
For each color, write the first feelings, memories or ideas that come to you before you read the traditional meaning.
Now read the traditional meanings and note where they match your own and where they differ.
Where they differ, choose which meaning you will use, or note both for different situations.
Pick one color you feel strongly about, light a candle of that color in a safe holder, and sit with it for five minutes.
Write down how that color felt in practice, then snuff the candle.
Revisit your key every few months as your practice grows.

variations.name: Two-color work
variations.text: Burn two candles side by side, such as green and gold for money and success, or pink and red for romance with passion. Some shops sell double-action candles that are two colors in one, often used to turn back one thing and draw in another.

variations.name: Color by planet
variations.text: Choose candles by planet: gold or yellow for the Sun, silver or white for the Moon, red for Mars, yellow or orange for Mercury, purple or royal blue for Jupiter, green or pink for Venus, and black or dark blue for Saturn.

variations.name: White plus a symbol
variations.text: When you only have white candles, carve a symbol or word that names the color you wanted, or set a crystal or ribbon of that color beside the holder (never touching the flame).

tools: Candles in the colors you use most, or a stock of white candles
Holders and a heatproof plate
Your journal
Optional: crystals or ribbons in matching colors to place beside the candle

As always, never leave a burning candle unattended, keep it at least 12 inches from anything that can burn, and keep it out of reach of children and pets.

title: Cleansing and Charging a Candle
subtitle: Clearing a candle and filling it with purpose
intro: A candle passes through many hands before it reaches yours: the maker, the shipper, the shop clerk and perhaps other shoppers. Many practitioners like to clear that leftover energy before working with a candle, so it becomes a blank slate for their own intention. This is called cleansing.

Charging is the second step. Once the candle is clear, you fill it with your purpose by holding it, focusing on your goal and imagining your energy flowing into the wax. Some practitioners also call this "loading" or "fixing" the candle, especially in hoodoo, where fixing usually includes dressing it with oil and herbs as well.

Neither step needs to be elaborate. A quick pass through incense smoke and a minute of focused breath while holding the candle is a complete practice. What matters most is that you are present and clear about what the candle is for.
keyIdeas: Cleansing removes leftover energy, and charging fills the candle with your intention.
Smoke cleansing, sound, visualization, salt and moonlight are all common ways to cleanse a candle.
Avoid soaking candles in water or salt water, which can dampen the wick and make it hard to light.
Charging can be as simple as holding the candle, breathing and picturing your goal already achieved.
Many practitioners charge a candle right before using it, so the intention is fresh.
Speaking your intention aloud while charging helps you clarify exactly what you want.

practice.name: Cleanse and Charge a Spell Candle
steps: Wash and dry your hands, and choose a candle for a specific intention.
Light a stick of cleansing incense in a safe holder, or ring a bell, and pass the unlit candle through the smoke or sound three times.
As you do, say something like "I clear this candle of all energies that are not my own."
Set the incense safely aside, then hold the candle in both hands at heart level.
Close your eyes, breathe slowly, and picture your goal as already real, with as much sensory detail as you can.
Imagine that feeling flowing down your arms and into the wax as a warm, glowing light.
State your intention clearly, for example "This candle brings steady, honest work into my life."
Place the candle on a pentacle, your altar, or a clean cloth until you are ready to use it, and note in your journal what it is for.

variations.name: Salt bed
variations.text: Lay the unlit candle in a dry dish of salt overnight. Many practitioners believe salt draws out unwanted energy. Brush it off well before lighting, and toss or bury the used salt rather than cooking with it.

variations.name: Moonlight charge
variations.text: Set the candle near a window under the full moon overnight to charge it with lunar energy. Bring it back to your altar before lighting it, since lit candles never go in windows.

variations.name: Crystal and breath
variations.text: Hold a piece of clear quartz or selenite with the candle while charging, or set the candle in a ring of crystals. Some witches simply breathe three times onto the candle while speaking their wish.

tools: Cleansing incense or a bell
A dish of dry salt (optional)
Clear quartz or selenite (optional)
A pentacle tile or clean altar cloth
Your journal

correspondences.label: Timing
correspondences.value: Waning or dark moon for cleansing, waxing or full moon for charging

correspondences.label: Herbs
correspondences.value: Rosemary, common sage and lavender for cleansing smoke

correspondences.label: Crystals
correspondences.value: Selenite and clear quartz to clear and amplify

correspondences.label: Oils
correspondences.value: A blessing oil once the candle is cleansed, or a Florida water style wash (let it dry fully)

correspondences.label: Symbols
correspondences.value: The pentacle as a charging plate

correspondences.label: Words
correspondences.value: "Cleared of all that is not mine, filled with what I name."

signs: The candle feels "yours" and ready when you pick it up.
You feel calmer and more focused when the spell begins.
Your intention is easier to put into words after the charging step.
pitfalls: Soaking a candle in water or moon water. A damp wick may not light well.
Skipping the charge and rushing straight to lighting, so the spell feels unfocused.
Charging a candle with a vague or conflicting intention.
Leaving a candle in a hot window, where wax can soften, warp or melt.
safety: If you cleanse with incense or a smoke bundle, burn it in a heatproof holder, ventilate the room, and never leave it smoldering unattended. Florida water and similar colognes are alcohol-based and highly flammable, so let them dry completely before any flame is near, and never light a candle that is still wet. Keep salt and crystals away from pets that might lick them, and wash your hands after handling herbs or oils. Do not leave unlit candles in hot windows, and remember that a lit candle never goes on a windowsill.

title: Carving and Inscribing
subtitle: Names, sigils, runes, symbols and numbers
intro: Carving words and symbols into a candle is one of the oldest and most personal ways to direct candle magic. As you carve, you spell out exactly what the candle is for, and many practitioners believe the message is released as the wax melts. It also slows you down, giving you a few minutes of focused intention before the flame is ever lit.

You can carve almost anything: your name or the name of the person you are working for (with their permission), an intention word such as "peace," a birth date, a dollar amount, runes, planetary glyphs, astrological signs or a sigil you designed yourself. In hoodoo rootwork it is common to carve a name and a short command, then dress the candle with oil.

Keep carvings simple and shallow. A few clear marks are more effective, and safer, than a crowded surface. Deep grooves can weaken the candle or change how it burns, and loose wax shavings near the wick can flare.
keyIdeas: Carving puts your intention into words or symbols and focuses your mind while you work.
Common carvings include names, birth dates, intention words, numbers, runes, planetary glyphs and personal sigils.
Only carve another person's name for work they have agreed to, or for blessings and healing they would welcome.
Many practitioners carve from the top of the candle downward for drawing work, and from the bottom upward for banishing.
A toothpick, pin, nail or blunt stylus works well. Warm the tool gently in your hand, not in a flame.
Keep marks shallow, especially near the top, and keep shavings away from the wick.
Save wax shavings to add to a petition packet or mojo-style bag, or dispose of them with the spell remains.

practice.name: Carve a Sigil Candle
steps: Write a short positive intention, such as "I attract new clients," or choose a ready-made symbol from the app's sigils.
If you are making your own sigil, cross out repeated letters and join the remaining shapes into a single design. Practice drawing it on paper.
Set a clean taper or pillar on a towel on a stable table, so it cannot roll.
Hold the candle steady by its base and carve with a toothpick or blunt pin, always moving the tool away from your holding hand.
Carve your name or initials near the bottom, the sigil in the middle, and leave the top half inch plain.
Brush loose shavings into a small dish and keep them away from the wick.
Hold the carved candle, trace the sigil with a fingertip, and state your intention aloud.
Place the candle in its holder on a heatproof plate, light it and focus on the sigil as it melts, snuffing it whenever you need to step away.

variations.name: Spiral carving
variations.text: Carve a spiral line from the top of the candle down to the base for drawing work, or from the base to the top for releasing, repeating your intention as the line circles the candle.

variations.name: Runes and glyphs
variations.text: Carve a single rune that fits the goal, such as Fehu for wealth, Algiz for protection or Sowilo for success, or a planetary glyph like Venus for love or Jupiter for growth.

variations.name: Glass-jar candles
variations.text: Jar candles cannot be carved on the side. Many practitioners carve a small symbol into the top surface away from the wick, or write the intention on paper and set it under the jar on the heatproof plate.

tools: A toothpick, pin, nail, blunt stylus or carving tool
A taper, chime or pillar candle
A towel or cloth to steady the candle
Paper and pen for designing sigils
A small dish for wax shavings

correspondences.label: Runes

correspondences.label: Planetary glyphs

correspondences.label: Symbols
correspondences.value: Pentacle for protection, spiral for growth, heart for love

correspondences.label: Numbers
correspondences.value: A specific dollar amount, a date, or a count of days for the goal

correspondences.label: Direction
correspondences.value: Top to bottom to draw, bottom to top to banish (one common tradition)

correspondences.label: Timing
correspondences.value: Waxing moon for drawing carvings, waning moon for banishing carvings

signs: Carving feels meditative and helps you settle into the spell.
The candle burns evenly through your carving without large drips or flare-ups.
You find yourself thinking of the symbol through the day after the spell.
pitfalls: Carving toward your fingers or using a sharp blade with a slippery grip.
Carving deep grooves near the top, which can make the candle drip, tunnel or break.
Cramming too many words and symbols onto one small candle.
Carving someone's name into a spell aimed at their free will without their consent.
safety: Always carve away from your hand using a toothpick, pin or blunt tool, and steady the candle on a towel so it cannot roll. Never heat your carving tool in an open flame, since a hot metal tool can burn you and melt the candle unevenly. Keep carvings shallow and leave the top half inch plain, brush shavings away from the wick, and never add paper, glitter or plastic to the candle itself. Glass-jar candles should not be scratched on the glass with metal tools, since a weakened jar can crack when hot. Keep sharp tools away from children and pets.

title: Dressing and Anointing
subtitle: Oils, directions and herbs, used safely
intro: Dressing a candle means rubbing it with oil, and sometimes adding a little powdered herb or curio, to align it with your goal. The oil carries the scent and properties of its herbs, and the act of rubbing it in is itself a focused, hands-on prayer. In hoodoo rootwork, dressing is a central part of fixing a candle, and many of the formula oils you will find in this app, such as Van Van, Road Opener, Money Drawing, Come to Me, Uncrossing and Fiery Wall of Protection, come from that African American tradition. Learn about their history from hoodoo practitioners and honor the culture they come from.

Direction matters to many practitioners, though traditions differ. One common method is to rub toward yourself to draw something in and away from yourself to send something away. Another is to rub from the top to the middle and then the bottom to the middle to draw, and from the middle outward to both ends to banish. Some witches simply rub from top to bottom to bring energy down into the physical world. Choose one method and use it consistently so it becomes meaningful to you.

Less is more. A few drops of oil, rubbed in well and the excess wiped away, is all a candle needs. Too much oil, or a thick coat of herbs, can make the flame flare, smoke heavily or even catch the side of the candle on fire. This lesson shows how to dress a candle so it is both effective and safe.
keyIdeas: Dressing aligns the candle with your goal through oil, scent and focused touch.
One tradition rubs toward you to draw and away from you to banish.
Another tradition rubs top to middle and bottom to middle to draw, and middle outward to banish.
Use only a few drops of oil, wipe off the excess, and keep oil off the wick and the top half inch.
Dilute essential oils in a carrier oil before they touch your skin, about a few drops in a teaspoon of carrier.
Herbs are a real fire risk: use only a light dusting of fine powder on the lower part, or ring the herbs around the base.
Formula oils such as Van Van and Road Opener come from hoodoo, an African American tradition that deserves respect and credit.

practice.name: Dress a Candle for Opening the Way
steps: Cleanse and charge a white or orange taper, and carve your name and a simple key or arrow symbol if you like.
Lay a paper towel on your work surface and set out Road Opener Oil or a carrier oil with a few drops of a diluted essential oil.
Put three or four drops of oil on your fingertips, not directly on the candle.
Hold the candle horizontally, wick pointing away from you, and rub the oil from the wick end toward yourself to draw open roads to you, keeping oil off the wick and the top half inch.
Repeat your intention as you rub, for example "All roads open before me."
Wipe off any extra oil with the paper towel until the candle feels only slightly slick.
If you want herbs, roll only the lower third of the candle very lightly in finely ground herb, or sprinkle a ring of herbs around the base on the heatproof plate instead.
Wash your hands well, then set the candle in a sturdy holder on a heatproof plate.
Light the candle and stay with it, keeping a snuffer or lid close in case the flame flares.

variations.name: Banishing dressing
variations.text: For removal or uncrossing work, use a black or white candle with Uncrossing Oil or Banishing Oil, and rub from the middle outward to both ends, or away from yourself, while naming what you are sending away.

variations.name: Glass-jar candle dressing
variations.text: For a 7-day jar candle, many practitioners poke three to five shallow holes in the top with a skewer, add a drop of oil to each, and place a small pinch of herb on top well away from the wick. Wipe the glass clean before lighting.

variations.name: Simple kitchen dressing
variations.text: Olive oil with a pinch of finely ground cinnamon works for money and success, and olive oil with a drop of diluted lavender oil works for peace. Kitchen oils are a perfectly traditional choice.

tools: A dressing oil or carrier oil (such as olive, jojoba or sweet almond)
Essential oils for blending, kept diluted
Finely ground dried herbs (optional)
Paper towels
A sturdy holder and heatproof plate
Soap and water for washing up

correspondences.label: To draw
correspondences.value: Toward you, or top to middle and bottom to middle

correspondences.label: To banish
correspondences.value: Away from you, or middle outward to both ends

correspondences.label: Money and luck
correspondences.value: Money Drawing Oil, cinnamon, basil

correspondences.label: Opening the way
correspondences.value: Road Opener Oil, Van Van Oil

correspondences.label: Love and attraction
correspondences.value: Come to Me Oil, rose, a little jasmine

correspondences.label: Protection and removal
correspondences.value: Fiery Wall of Protection Oil, Uncrossing Oil, Banishing Oil

correspondences.label: Blessing and peace
correspondences.value: Blessing Oil, lavender

correspondences.label: Carrier oils
correspondences.value: Olive, jojoba, sweet almond

signs: The candle feels pleasantly slick, not dripping, and smells of your oil.
The flame burns steady and clean without flaring.
Dressing becomes a calm, focused part of the ritual rather than a messy chore.
pitfalls: Pouring oil straight onto the candle, so it pools and flares.
Rolling the whole candle in a thick coat of herbs, which can catch fire.
Getting oil on the wick, which can make it sputter, smoke or flare.
Using undiluted essential oils on your skin.
Treating hoodoo formulas as generic "witch oils" without learning where they come from.
safety: Use only a few drops of dressing oil and wipe off the excess, keeping oil off the wick and the top half inch of the candle, because too much oil can make the flame flare. Rolling a candle in dried herbs is a real fire risk: use only a light dusting of finely ground herb on the lower part of a pillar or taper, sprinkle herbs in a ring around the base on the heatproof plate, or put a pinch on top of a glass-jar candle away from the wick. Watch the candle the whole time and keep a lid or snuffer and water nearby. Dilute essential oils (a few drops in a teaspoon of carrier oil), never use them on broken skin, and wash your hands after dressing. Keep candles and oils away from pets, since cats are especially sensitive to essential oils.
journal: Which dressing direction feels right to me, and why?
How did the candle burn when I used less oil versus more?
What do I know about the history of hoodoo formula oils, and where can I learn more from Black practitioners?

quiz.q: In one common tradition, rubbing oil toward yourself is used to:
Where should you keep oil off when dressing a candle?
options: The wick and the top half inch

quiz.q: What is the safest way to add herbs to a pillar or taper?
options: Roll the whole candle in a thick coat
A light dusting of fine powder on the lower part, or a ring around the base

quiz.q: Formula oils such as Van Van and Road Opener come from which tradition?

title: Timing Candle Magic
subtitle: Moon phases, weekdays and planetary hours
intro: Many witches time candle spells to natural cycles, believing that working with the right moon phase, day or hour adds momentum to the intention. Timing is a layer, like color or oil. It can strengthen a spell, but it is never required. A spell done at the "wrong" time with real focus is better than one put off for weeks.

The moon is the most popular timing tool. As it grows from new to full, it supports drawing and growth. As it shrinks from full to dark, it supports releasing and banishing. The full moon is a peak of power for almost anything, and the dark moon is a time for rest, shadow work and deep banishing.

Days of the week each carry a planet in the Western tradition, and the names often show it: Sunday for the Sun, Monday for the Moon, Saturday for Saturn. Planetary hours go one step further, dividing each day and night into twelve parts, each ruled by a planet. This lesson gives a brief overview so you can start simply and add detail as you go.
keyIdeas: Timing is an optional layer that many practitioners use to add momentum to a spell.
Waxing moon (new to full) supports drawing, growth and increase.
Full moon is a peak for power, completion, charging and divination.
Waning moon (full to dark) supports releasing, banishing and decrease; the dark moon suits rest and deep banishing.
Each day of the week is ruled by a planet with its own themes and colors.
Planetary hours divide daytime and nighttime into twelve unequal hours each, the first daytime hour ruled by the day's own planet.
Multi-day candle spells often begin on a matching day and moon phase and continue each day after.

practice.name: Plan a Timed Candle Spell
steps: Write down your intention and decide whether it is about drawing something in or sending something away.
Check the current moon phase in a moon calendar, and choose a waxing moon for drawing or a waning moon for releasing.
Pick a day of the week whose planet matches your goal, using the correspondences in this lesson.
If you like, look up the planetary hours for that day using your local sunrise and sunset, and choose an hour of the same planet.
Choose a candle color that matches the planet or the goal, or use white.
Mark the date and time in your calendar, and gather your candle and tools the day before.
Perform the spell at the chosen time, noting the moon phase, day and hour in your journal.
Over the next weeks, record results so you can see whether timing makes a difference for you.

variations.name: Just the moon
variations.text: If weekday and hour feel like too much, use only the moon phase. Growth when it waxes, release when it wanes is a complete and time-tested system.

variations.name: Just the day
variations.text: If you need to work right now, pick the best day this week, such as Friday for love or Thursday for growth, and skip the moon phase. Many practitioners work this way with good results.

variations.name: Turning the spell around
variations.text: If the moon phase does not match, reframe the goal. During a waning moon, a money spell can become "releasing debt" or "removing blocks to money" instead of "drawing money."

tools: A moon calendar or moon phase app
Your local sunrise and sunset times for planetary hours
A candle in a color matching the planet or goal
Your journal or planner

correspondences.label: Sunday (Sun)
correspondences.value: Success, vitality, fame, leadership; gold, yellow

correspondences.label: Monday (Moon)
correspondences.value: Intuition, dreams, home, emotions; silver, white

correspondences.label: Tuesday (Mars)
correspondences.value: Courage, strength, protection, conflict; red

correspondences.label: Wednesday (Mercury)
correspondences.value: Communication, study, travel, business; yellow, orange

correspondences.label: Thursday (Jupiter)
correspondences.value: Growth, luck, abundance, justice; purple, royal blue

correspondences.label: Friday (Venus)
correspondences.value: Love, friendship, beauty, harmony; green, pink

correspondences.label: Saturday (Saturn)
correspondences.value: Banishing, boundaries, endings, protection; black, dark blue

correspondences.label: Waxing moon
correspondences.value: Drawing, growth, increase, new projects

correspondences.label: Full moon
correspondences.value: Power, completion, charging, divination

correspondences.label: Waning and dark moon
correspondences.value: Releasing, banishing, cleansing, rest

correspondences.label: Planetary hour order
correspondences.value: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon, repeating

signs: Planning the timing builds anticipation and focus before the spell.
Your journal begins to show which phases and days work best for you.
You start noticing the moon and the days of the week as part of your daily rhythm.
pitfalls: Waiting weeks for perfect timing when the need is urgent.
Getting lost in planetary hour calculations and losing the spell's focus.
Forgetting that planetary hours are not 60 minutes long; they change length with the season.
Assuming every tradition uses the same correspondences. Some differ, and that is fine.
safety: Timing should never push you to burn a candle when you cannot watch it. If a planetary hour falls late at night, light the candle only if you will stay awake and present, and snuff it before you sleep. For multi-day spells, snuff the candle at the end of each session and relight it at the next; never leave it burning unattended overnight to "keep" the timing. As always, use a sturdy holder on a heatproof plate, at least 12 inches from anything that can burn, and out of reach of children and pets.
journal: Which moon phase do I feel most energized by?
Did timing my spell change how it felt or how it turned out?
Which weekday planet do I connect with most strongly?

quiz.q: Which moon phase is traditionally best for drawing things in?
Which day of the week is ruled by Venus?
The first planetary hour after sunrise is ruled by:
If the moon is waning but you need a money spell, you could:
options: Reframe it as releasing debt or removing blocks to money

title: Building a Candle Spell
subtitle: From intention to closing, step by step
intro: Now that you know how to choose, cleanse, carve and dress a candle, you can put the pieces together into a complete spell. Most candle spells, whether from Wicca, folk magic or hoodoo, follow the same basic shape: a clear intention, a prepared candle, a layout, spoken words, a focused burn and a clear closing.

A petition paper is a simple and powerful addition. You write your request on paper and place it under the candle holder or under the plate, so the candle "sits on" your request as it burns. In hoodoo rootwork, a common form is to write a name three times, turn the paper and write the command across it three times, then fold the paper toward you to draw or away from you to send away.

Your spell can be as simple or as layered as you like. Start with fewer elements and add more as you learn what works for you. Above all, back up the spell with real-world action: apply for the job, send the message, see the doctor. Magic tends to work through the openings you make.
keyIdeas: A candle spell usually follows the pattern: intention, preparation, layout, words, burning, closing.
Write your intention as a clear, positive, present-tense statement.
A petition paper goes under the holder or plate, never on or around the candle itself.
A layout can include crystals, herbs in a ring, photos or symbols around the candle, all kept clear of the flame.
Spoken words, whether a prayer, chant or simple statement, help focus and release your intention.
Many spells burn the candle in one sitting or across several sessions, snuffing between sessions.
Close the spell with thanks, record it in your journal, and take a practical step toward your goal.

practice.name: A Complete Candle Spell for a New Opportunity
steps: Write your intention in one sentence, such as "A good new job opportunity comes to me easily and quickly."
Choose an orange or green chime candle (or white), then cleanse, charge, carve and lightly dress it as you learned in earlier lessons.
On a small square of paper, write your name three times, turn the paper a quarter turn, and write "new opportunity" across your name three times. Fold the paper toward you.
Place the folded petition on a heatproof plate, set the holder on top of it, and put the candle in the holder.
Arrange a few crystals and a pinch of herbs in a ring around the base of the holder, keeping everything at least a few inches from the flame.
Ground and center, then light the candle and speak your intention, or a short chant such as "Doors open, paths clear, my new work draws near."
Sit with the flame, visualizing yourself already in the new role, for as long as you can stay focused and present.
Let the chime candle burn down while you watch, or snuff it and relight it at the next session until it is finished.
Thank the flame and any spirits or deities you work with, record the spell in your journal, and send at least one job application within the next day.

variations.name: Three-night spell
variations.text: Use a taper and mark it in three equal sections. Burn one section each night for three nights, snuffing between sessions and repeating your words each time.

variations.name: Seven-day jar spell
variations.text: Place your petition under a glass-jar candle and light it for an hour or two each day for seven days, praying or speaking your intention each time, until it has burned down to about 1/2 inch.

variations.name: Minimal spell
variations.text: A white tealight, a petition paper underneath and a sincere spoken intention is a complete spell when you are short on time or supplies.

tools: A prepared candle (cleansed, charged, carved and dressed)
Paper and a pen for your petition
A sturdy holder and heatproof plate or tray
Crystals, herbs, a photo or symbols for the layout (optional)
A snuffer or lid
Your journal

correspondences.label: Petition paper
correspondences.value: Plain brown paper bag or plain white paper; write in pen or pencil

correspondences.label: Folding
correspondences.value: Toward you to draw, away from you to send away

correspondences.label: Layout
correspondences.value: Crystals, herbs in a ring, symbols or photos, all kept clear of the flame

correspondences.label: Words
correspondences.value: A prayer, psalm, chant or simple present-tense statement

correspondences.label: Opportunity
correspondences.value: Orange or green candle, Road Opener Oil, bay leaf

correspondences.label: Timing
correspondences.value: Waxing moon, or a weekday that matches the goal

signs: You feel a sense of completion and calm when the spell ends.
The candle burns cleanly and steadily through your sessions.
Opportunities, ideas or conversations related to your goal begin to appear.
pitfalls: Writing a vague or conflicting intention, such as wanting a job and wanting to stay home at once.
Putting the petition paper or herbs too close to the flame.
Leaving the candle to burn "to completion" while you sleep or go out.
Doing the spell and then taking no real-world action toward the goal.
Repeating the same spell every day out of worry instead of giving it time to work.
safety: If a spell traditionally burns the candle "to completion," snuff it (do not blow it out) whenever you need to leave or sleep, and relight it at the next session. Keep the petition paper under the holder or plate, never touching the candle or the flame, and keep layout herbs and crystals in a ring a few inches from the base. Use a sturdy holder on a heatproof plate or tray, at least 12 inches from curtains, paper, plants and anything that can burn, out of reach of children and pets, and tie back long hair and loose sleeves. Keep a snuffer or lid and water nearby, but never throw water on hot wax or a wax fire.
journal: What exactly did I ask for, and how did I word it?
Which parts of the spell felt most powerful, and which felt unnecessary?
What real-world steps did I take after the spell, and what happened?

quiz.q: Where does a petition paper go in a candle spell?
In one hoodoo method, a petition is folded toward you in order to:
What should you do with a "burn to completion" candle when you need to go to bed?
options: Snuff it and relight it at the next session
Blow it out and throw it away

quiz.q: What is the final step of a good candle spell?
options: Closing with thanks, journaling and taking real-world action

title: Reading the Flame and the Wax
subtitle: Ceromancy: traditional signs and their physical causes
intro: Many practitioners watch how a spell candle burns and treat its behavior as a message about the spell. Reading the flame is sometimes called pyromancy or lychnomancy, and reading melted wax is called ceromancy. In European folk practice, people dripped hot wax into cold water and read the shapes that formed, and in hoodoo rootwork, workers often read the soot, the flame and the wax left behind after a candle has burned.

These readings are traditional interpretations, not laws of nature. A flickering flame might be read as spirits drawing near, but it is also exactly what happens in a draft. Black soot might be read as negativity being burned away, but it also comes from a long wick, too much oil or dyed wax. A good reader notices both the physical cause and their own intuition.

The fairest way to read a candle is to remove the physical causes you can control first: trim the wick, use a modest amount of oil, close the window and keep the candle away from vents and fans. Then whatever still stands out may be worth reflecting on. Keep notes, and over time you will build your own personal language of flame and wax.
keyIdeas: Ceromancy is reading wax; reading the flame is sometimes called pyromancy or lychnomancy.
Readings are traditional interpretations, and physical causes such as drafts, wick length and oil should always be considered too.
A strong, steady flame is traditionally read as the spell working well, and a weak or low flame as resistance or slow progress.
A jumping or flickering flame is often read as active energy or spirit presence, and is also a classic sign of a draft.
Heavy black smoke or soot is often read as resistance or negativity being burned off, and physically comes from a long wick, too much oil or incomplete burning.
Wax shapes, drips and leftover puddles can be read like tea leaves, looking for symbols that stand out to you.
Your journal is the best guide: patterns in your own readings matter more than any list.

practice.name: A Fair Flame Reading
steps: Before the spell, trim the wick to about 1/4 inch, close windows, and move the candle away from vents, fans and doorways.
Dress the candle lightly, keeping oil off the wick, so physical causes are kept to a minimum.
Light the candle, state your intention, and let the flame settle for a minute or two.
Observe the flame's height, steadiness, color and any sounds such as crackling or popping, and write them down.
Notice any smoke, which way the wax melts and drips, and whether the candle burns evenly.
For each observation, write both the traditional reading from this lesson and any possible physical cause.
Snuff the candle when you finish or need to leave, and once the remains are completely cool, look at the wax for shapes or symbols.
Record your impressions, then compare them with how the situation actually unfolds over the next weeks.

variations.name: Wax in water
variations.text: Let a lit candle melt a little, then carefully tip a few drops of wax into a bowl of cool water. Read the shapes that form, much as you would read tea leaves. Keep the bowl on a stable surface and never pour wax down the drain afterward.

variations.name: Glass-jar soot reading
variations.text: In hoodoo practice, workers often read the glass of a 7-day candle when it finishes: clean, clear glass is commonly read as a smooth result, while heavy black soot is commonly read as obstacles or opposition. Soot near the top only may be read as early resistance that cleared.

variations.name: Two-candle reading
variations.text: Burn two identical candles for two choices or two people, side by side and away from drafts, and compare how each burns. Many practitioners read the steadier or longer-burning candle as the stronger path.

tools: A spell candle in a sturdy holder on a heatproof plate
Wick trimmer or small scissors
A bowl of cool water (for wax reading)
Your journal and a pen
Optional: divination incense or a psychic vision oil for focus

correspondences.label: Strong, steady flame
correspondences.value: Traditionally: the spell is working smoothly. Physically: a well-trimmed wick and still air

correspondences.label: Weak or low flame
correspondences.value: Traditionally: resistance or slow progress. Physically: a short or drowned wick, or a wide melt pool

correspondences.label: High, tall flame
correspondences.value: Traditionally: lots of energy and quick results. Physically: a long wick or too much oil

correspondences.label: Flickering or dancing
correspondences.value: Traditionally: spirits near or energy moving. Physically: a draft, vent or movement in the room

correspondences.label: Crackling or popping
correspondences.value: Traditionally: messages or interference. Physically: moisture, air pockets, herbs or oil in the wax

correspondences.label: Black smoke or soot
correspondences.value: Traditionally: resistance or negativity burning off. Physically: a long wick, too much oil, or dyed wax

correspondences.label: Wick mushrooming
correspondences.value: Traditionally: extra power building up. Physically: carbon buildup on a long wick

correspondences.label: Flame goes out
correspondences.value: Traditionally: the spell is finished or blocked. Physically: a drowned wick or a draft; relight if you wish

correspondences.label: Jar glass cracks
correspondences.value: Traditionally in hoodoo: strong opposition or a spell that needs redoing. Physically: heat stress

correspondences.label: Wax shapes
correspondences.value: Hearts for love, circles for completion, paths or lines for travel or roads opening, read by your intuition

signs: You start to notice the difference between a draft flicker and a flicker in still air.
Your notes begin to show patterns between how candles burn and how situations turn out.
Wax shapes start to suggest symbols to you more easily.
pitfalls: Panicking over one sooty candle or a dancing flame without checking the wick or the air in the room.
Treating every reading as a certain prediction rather than one piece of insight.
Using a reading as a reason to leave a candle burning unattended to "see what happens."
Forgetting to record readings, so you never learn your own patterns.
safety: A tall, jumping or smoking flame is a reading, but it is also a safety warning. If a flame grows high, flares or smokes heavily, snuff it, let the candle cool, trim the wick to 1/4 inch and wipe away excess oil before relighting. Glass-jar candles can crack or shatter from heat, so keep them on a heatproof surface, never in a window, and do not let them burn dry. Ventilate the room when candles smoke. When dripping wax into water, use a stable bowl and work slowly so hot wax does not splash your skin, and never pour wax down a drain. Never leave a candle burning unattended to watch how it ends.
journal: What did the flame do during my last spell, and what physical causes might explain it?
Which readings turned out to match what happened?
What shapes did I see in the wax, and what did they mean to me?

quiz.q: What is ceromancy?
A flame flickering wildly in a room with an open window is most likely caused by:
Which physical cause often produces black soot?
options: A long wick or too much oil

quiz.q: Before reading a flame fairly, you should:
options: Trim the wick and keep the candle out of drafts

title: Candle Safety, Snuffing and Disposal
subtitle: Ending the flame and the spell with care
intro: Candles cause thousands of home fires every year, and most of them start when a candle is left unattended, placed too close to something that burns, or knocked over. Safe habits are not a distraction from magic; they are part of treating Fire with the respect it deserves. A spell that burns your home down has not gone well.

How you put out a candle matters to many practitioners. A common belief is that blowing out a spell candle disrespects the element of Fire or blows the spell's energy away, so most witches snuff spell candles instead, using a snuffer, a lid or a wick dipper. Others are comfortable blowing candles out, especially in traditions where breath carries a wish, such as birthday candles. Choose what fits your practice, but snuffing is also safer, since it avoids splattering hot wax.

When a spell is finished, what is left behind, such as wax, petition papers and herbs, still carries meaning. Many practitioners keep the remains of drawing spells, bury the remains of spells for growth, and take banishing remains away from the home. Whatever you choose, let everything cool completely, and dispose of it in a way that is respectful to both the spell and the environment.
keyIdeas: Never leave a burning candle unattended or burning while you sleep.
Use a sturdy holder on a heatproof plate, at least 12 inches from anything that can burn, out of reach of children and pets.
Many practitioners snuff spell candles rather than blowing them out, out of respect for Fire and to avoid splattering wax.
A candle that traditionally burns "to completion" can be snuffed and relit at the next session.
Never throw water on hot wax or a wax fire; smother it with a lid or snuffer instead.
Let remains cool completely, then keep, bury, bin or remove them from your home as the spell suggests.
Never pour hot wax down a drain, and avoid dumping wax, paraffin or glass into soil, rivers or the ocean.

practice.name: Closing and Clearing a Finished Spell
steps: When the spell is done, or you need to leave, lower a snuffer gently over the flame, or dip the wick into the melted wax and lift it back up with a wick dipper.
Say a short closing, such as "The flame rests, the work goes on. Thank you."
Leave the candle and holder exactly where they are until the wax is completely cool and hard, at least an hour for large candles.
Look over the remains and note anything you want to read in your journal.
Gather the cool wax, petition paper and herbs onto a paper towel or into a small bag.
For drawing spells, keep the remains in a jar or packet on your altar until your goal arrives; for banishing spells, take them away from your home and place them in an outside trash bin.
For glass-jar candles, place the cooled jar in the freezer for a few hours so the leftover wax pops out, then wash the glass and recycle or cleanse and reuse it.
Wipe down your holder and plate, wash your hands, and cleanse the space with incense or a quick sweep if you like.

variations.name: Burying remains
variations.text: For growth, healing or blessing spells, many practitioners bury natural remains, such as herbs, plain paper and pure beeswax, in the garden or a potted plant. Put paraffin wax, metal tea light cups and glass in the trash or recycling instead.

variations.name: Crossroads disposal
variations.text: In hoodoo rootwork, the remains of banishing or uncrossing work are traditionally left at a crossroads, then the worker walks away without looking back. A respectful modern version is to drop them in a public trash can near an intersection, rather than littering.

variations.name: Wet fingers and other ways
variations.text: Some practitioners pinch out a small flame with wet fingertips or cover a jar candle with its lid. A snuffer is gentlest and safest, but any method that smothers the flame without splattering wax works.

tools: A candle snuffer, wick dipper or metal lid
A sturdy holder and heatproof plate or tray
A small fire extinguisher or a box of baking soda for emergencies
Paper towels and a small bag or jar for remains
A wick trimmer

correspondences.label: Drawing spells
correspondences.value: Keep the remains in a jar or packet until the goal arrives

correspondences.label: Growth and blessing
correspondences.value: Bury natural remains (beeswax, herbs, plain paper) in soil or a plant pot

correspondences.label: Banishing and uncrossing
correspondences.value: Remove from home; trash bin away from the house or near a crossroads

correspondences.label: Glass jars
correspondences.value: Freeze to release wax, wash, then recycle or cleanse and reuse

correspondences.label: Herbs
correspondences.value: Rosemary or common sage for cleansing the space afterward

correspondences.label: Crystals
correspondences.value: Black tourmaline or smoky quartz on the altar for grounding after banishing work

signs: Your altar stays clean and safe, with no wax spills or scorch marks.
Closing a spell feels as intentional as opening it.
Disposing of remains gives you a clear sense that the work is complete and released.
pitfalls: Leaving a candle to burn overnight because the spell says to burn it all at once.
Throwing water on a pan of hot wax or a wax fire, which can make the fire explode outward.
Moving a lit candle or a jar full of liquid wax.
Pouring melted wax down the sink, where it hardens and clogs pipes.
Leaving wax, glass or plastic at a real crossroads or in a river, which harms wildlife and neighbors.
safety: Never leave a burning candle unattended or burning while you sleep, and keep candles at least 12 inches from curtains, paper, plants and anything that can burn, out of reach of children and pets. Snuff flames rather than blowing them out, which can spray hot wax. Never throw water on hot wax or a wax fire: smother it with a lid, a snuffer or baking soda, and call emergency services if a fire spreads. Do not move a candle while it is lit or while the wax is liquid. Glass-jar candles can crack when hot, so never let them burn dry or set them in a window. Once the wax is completely cool, dispose of it respectfully, and never pour hot wax down a drain. Keep dressing oils and remains away from pets, since cats are especially sensitive to essential oils.
journal: Do I snuff or blow out my candles, and what does that choice mean to me?
How do I want to dispose of remains for drawing spells versus banishing spells?
Which candle safety habits do I need to work on?

quiz.q: Why do many practitioners snuff spell candles instead of blowing them out?
options: Out of respect for Fire and to avoid splattering wax
